newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems harassed in Serb, Croat parts of Bosnia-UN.
newsitem.headline: Moslems harassed in Serb, Croat parts of Bosnia-UN.

text.p: The United Nations said on Friday that Moslems in the Bosnian Serb town of Teslic and the Croat sector of Mostar were being pressured to leave through a campaign of harassment and verbal intimidation.
"We had seven to eight cases of intimidation in Teslic in the past two weeks, which involve harassment and burning of haystacks," spokesman Alex Ivanko said.
Teslic is a town in northern Bosnia controlled by the Bosnian Serbs which saw most of its Moslem and Croat residents expelled during the course of the 43-month war.
Before the war began in 1992 non-Serbs numbered about 40 percent of the Teslic population according to a census. About 1,000 Moslems still live there, Ivanko said.
The U.N. in Teslic was told on Thursday about the kidnapping of a Moslem man by two uniformed Serbs, he added.
The U.N. international police tracked the man down in Serb police custody, where he had been charged with "shouting Moslem propaganda while being drunk".
"We believe that this is absolutely unacceptable that the minorities are once again being pressured to leave the Teslic area," Ivanko said.

In the divided Bosnian town of Mostar a Moslem woman complained to U.N. police that she was receiving threatening phone calls, pressuring her to leave her flat in the Croat part of town. She had been expelled from her flat on February 10 but returned five days ago with the help of international organisations.

Fighting in Bosnia ended with a U.S.-brokered peace agreement in December 1995 but Serb and Croat nationalists have since continued the policy of creating ethnically pure areas, uprooting hundreds of people.
The U.N. estimates some 250,000 have returned to their homes, but mainly to areas where they form a majority. Minority returns have not been significant.
Kris Janowski, spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, said living conditions for non-Serbs in the Bosnian Serb part of the country are very difficult.
"We had a wave of expulsions from Teslic and Banja Luka last summer, when about 100 people were expelled from Teslic only," he said.
Janowski said the last expulsions were preceded by similar harassment, but could not predict if more expulsions could be expected. "We have to wait and see," he said.
The pressure on the Moslem minority in Serb and Croat areas will not help the issue of refugee returns, Ivanko said.
"There are areas in Bosnia where the situation for Moslems is not easy, to say the least, and when Moslems are pressured to leave, it only makes the refugee situation more difficult."

A western official said he believed Bosnian Serbs wanted to take advantage of the media focus on Moslem-Croat relations since a group of Moslems was attacked while visiting a cemetery in the Croat part of Mostar on February 10.
"My reading is that Serbs probably think they have a chance now to quietly push a few people out," an official, who asked not to be named, said.
